01.r: Asks the hearers to choose between the two sons of the parable.

05.r: Which son actually carried out what was asked.
05.n: Abbott-Smith notes that in the Septuagint this verb chiefly translates Hebrew עשׂה, to do or make.

06.r: The particular will the father expressed.

07.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is objective: 'that which is willed'.

08.r: The article, in the genitive; English 'of' comes from the case.
08.n: The Greek says 'the father'; the KJV, ASV and BSB say 'his father'.

10.r: The hearers give their answer, in the present tense.

12.r: Picks out one of the two sons.

13.r: The first son of the parable.
13.n: Who the first son is comes from the parable before this verse.

14.r: Jesus answers them, in the present tense of a past narrative.

15.r: The hearers who have just answered.

16.r: Greek often puts the article before a personal name; English does not.

18.r: Puts solemn weight on what follows.
18.n: A Hebrew word kept in the Greek. Abbott-Smith derives it from a Hebrew root meaning to be firm. This study keeps the word itself, as the DRC does.

22.r: The toll collectors as a class.

23.n: This study renders the word 'toll collector' throughout.

26.r: Women who sold sex, named alongside the toll collectors.
26.n: Abbott-Smith defines it as 'a prostitute, harlot' and cites this verse. In the Septuagint it chiefly answers to Hebrew זָנָה.

27.r: They are on the way in ahead of the leaders who were asked.
27.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense of the verb is transitive, 'to lead on, lead forth or forward'; here, with 'you' as its object, it means to go ahead of. The present tense says it is already happening; the DRC's 'shall go' makes it future. Whether 'ahead of' implies the leaders follow later is not said.

30.r: Part of the phrase 'the kingdom of God'.

31.r: God's rule, entered as one enters a realm.
31.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is abstract, 'sovereignty, royal power, dominion', which the YLT's 'reign' keeps. Here 'go into' treats it as a realm one can enter.

32.r: The article before 'God'; English leaves it out.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus adds αὐτῷ, 'to him', after 'they say'. That is why the KJV reads 'They say unto him' (with the Geneva, DRC and YLT); the ASV and BSB, following our text, have no 'to him'.
